job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Aisha Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in a shared flat near Marlow University with two other postgraduates. Mornings I'm in a data science master's seminar, then I write code for my dissertation on delivery routes, which grew out of a ten-week internship at a logistics firm called Tamsin Freight. Afternoons I tutor first-years in programming for 14 an hour. My debt is around 28,000 and I've got maybe three weeks of rent in my account, and no one at home can help with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, that fits what I see. The AI helpers I use are useful for boring bits like writing test cases, but they get things wrong often enough that I always check. I'd probably say that to my coding society friends and add that the hype is exhausting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my worry stays the same. There are very few data jobs near Marlow, about five graduate roles a year, and I'm one of forty applicants for each. A flat world doesn't make that better. I'd still be in the same queue, with the same debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my dissertation, keep tutoring and apply to roughly 50 jobs, including a few in the capital where I'd have to share a room. I'd try to turn my dissertation into a portfolio piece, because it shows I can handle real delivery data. I'd also ask Tamsin Freight if they'd take me on for summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, honestly. Not scared, not happy, just tired and watching the bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use them for writing test cases and explaining error messages, maybe twice a week. I never paste in anything for my dissertation without understanding it, because my supervisor, Dr Basu, would spot it straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what is the thing you'd still lose sleep over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, then the queue. I can survive on tutoring for about four months after the course ends, and after that I'd be borrowing. So I'd say job offers first, and any offer, even a poor one, is better than waiting.

say: I'd say the tools are **useful but wrong often**, and the hype is exhausting.
I'd tell my coding society that the real problem is **too few jobs** nearby.
think: Privately my worry stays the same: about **five graduate roles** a year near Marlow.
I'm one of forty applicants for each, with **28,000 debt** behind me.
do: Apply to **50 jobs**, including a few in the capital.
Turn my dissertation into a **portfolio piece** on delivery routes.
feel: **Flat** and tired, watching the bank balance.
S0.quote: A flat world doesn't make that better. I'd still be in the same queue, with the same debt.
fieldNote: Aisha's anxiety is **structural**: few local openings and debt, with or without AI.
She uses AI sensibly and verifies it, a typical steady adopter.
Her tutoring income gives about four months of runway, which she counts exactly.

steps.text: Apply to 50 data and software jobs, including three in the capital
Turn the delivery routes dissertation into a portfolio project
Keep tutoring first-years at 14 an hour through the summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and it's already visible in the job ads. Fewer junior roles, more ads asking for experience with AI tools. I'd tell people on my course to stop treating the tools as cheating and learn them properly, because refusing won't protect anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think the junior data job is the thing that shrinks. Cleaning data, writing reports, building dashboards, that was most of my ten weeks at Tamsin Freight. If software does that, a company needs one senior person instead of four juniors, and I've seen it start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend this year getting properly good with the tools, not just using them now and then. I'd do an online course on building AI workflows, around 60 for a certificate, and put two real projects on my page. I'd also apply early to graduate schemes that hire in groups, since they're the last ones keeping juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix of nervous and challenged. I'd be pushed to get better, which I don't hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a junior data job do you expect software to take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cleaning messy delivery data, writing weekly summary reports and making dashboards. My team lead Ruth said the report writing was 'the bit nobody will miss', and now I'm not sure that was a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who tells you to just learn the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I agree, but learning the tools doesn't create the jobs. If a company needs one person where it needed four, the other three can be excellent and still be out. Learning tools makes me better placed, but it doesn't make the queue shorter.

say: I'd tell my course that refusing the tools **protects no one**, so learn them properly.
I'd say the **junior roles** are already shrinking in the job ads.
think: Cleaning data and writing reports was my internship, so the **entry job** is what shrinks.
One senior person can replace **four juniors**, and I've seen it start.
do: Take a **60 certificate** course on building AI workflows this autumn.
Put **two real projects** on my portfolio page and apply to group graduate schemes.
feel: **Nervous** but challenged, pushed to get better.
S1.quote: If a company needs one person where it needed four, the other three can be excellent and still be out.
fieldNote: Aisha takes the change seriously and answers with **skills**, but sees the limit of that answer.
Her internship tasks map straight onto what software takes first.
She names graduate schemes as the last place that hires in numbers.

steps.text: Take a 60 certificate course on building AI workflows this autumn
Add two real projects to the online portfolio before applying
Apply early to group graduate schemes that hire in September

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules now, not in five years. The last time something this big arrived, regulators were slow and ordinary people paid. I'd post that and join any group campaigning for a plan on jobs and income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my path closes. The degree I chose is the thing AGI does first, and the timing is brutal: I'd just be starting. I'd have 28,000 of debt and be competing with something that works for the price of electricity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop planning for a career in data and look for anything with a person in it. Care work, teaching assistant jobs, anything that's paid. I'd ask the university about hardship funds, and move home to my aunt's spare room in Calder, about 90 miles away, to stop paying rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like standing on a platform and the timetable's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the dissertation if two years was real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put it in a drawer, honestly. If the thing it's about gets done by AI anyway, then it's worth a pass mark and no more. I'd still hand it in, because the loan paperwork needs me enrolled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt, my friend Lena (a flatmate on my course) and the hardship office. And a union, if one existed for graduates. I wouldn't lean on my parents, who live on a pension and would hand me everything they have, which I couldn't take.

say: I'd say we need **rules now**, because regulators were slow last time and ordinary people paid.
I'd join any group pushing for a **jobs and income plan**.
think: The degree I chose is what AGI does **first**, and I'd be just starting.
I'd be competing with something that works for the price of **electricity**.
do: Look for work with a **person in it**, such as teaching assistant or care jobs.
Apply to the university **hardship fund** and move to my aunt's room in Calder.
feel: **Scared**, like standing on a platform when the timetable is gone.
S2.quote: I'd have 28,000 of debt and be competing with something that works for the price of electricity.
fieldNote: Aisha drops her field altogether; her fallback is **human-contact work**.
Moving to her aunt's room is a rent decision, not a lifestyle one.
She refuses to lean on her parents, who would give everything.

steps.text: Apply for teaching assistant and care jobs near Calder
Apply to the university hardship fund and ask about the loan
Move into my aunt's spare room in Calder to end rent
Join a graduate group campaigning for a jobs and income plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is just enough to do something about it, if we move now. I'd push for retraining funds and a rule that companies that cut staff report it. I'd say it loudly and keep saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I think I can build something. I'd have the master's, maybe a couple of years of real work and a chance to move into the kind of job that's about deciding and explaining, not just writing code. It's still frightening, but I have a map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first decent data job, even if it's mediocre, and learn how an actual company works. I'd save about 150 a month and pay the debt down faster than the minimum. In year two I'd look at moving toward the human end of the job, like being the person who explains the results to a client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less scared than before. Uneasy, but I can see a route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you if you have five years rather than two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings above all. A six-month cushion would let me say no to a bad offer or survive a gap, and I've never had that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have in place by the end of those five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At least a year of real experience, a cushion of 3,000, and a role where people trust me with their questions, not just their data. That's what I'd try to build.

say: I'd push for **retraining funds** and a rule that firms report staff cuts.
I'd say five years is **just enough** if we start now.
think: With five years I can **build something**: the master's, real work and a move toward explaining results.
It's still frightening, but I have a **map**.
do: Take the **first decent data job** and save 150 a month.
In year two, move toward **client-facing** work that explains results.
feel: **Uneasy** but with a route, less scared than with two years.
S3.quote: A six-month cushion would let me say no to a bad offer or survive a gap, and I've never had that.
fieldNote: Time lets Aisha trade panic for a **plan**: save, learn, move to the human end of the job.
Still anxious because the first job is not secured.

steps.text: Take the first decent data job and learn how the firm works
Save 150 a month toward a 3,000 cushion
Ask to shadow the account team presenting results to clients
Write to my representative about retraining funds for graduates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the one scenario where we can get it right. Ten years is long enough for training systems and income rules. I'd still say we shouldn't wait, because decades-long plans tend to slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is enough to have a real career first. I could be 34 with a senior role and a bit of savings, and the AI would be one more tool changing the job. I'd be careful, but I wouldn't be afraid in the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job, keep learning one new tool every couple of months and build a name in one area, like transport data. I'd aim to get the debt below 10,000 within five years. I'd probably also start a part-time degree in something human-facing, maybe psychology, to have two feet in the water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, actually. Anxious in the background, but it's a normal anxiety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years let you do that two couldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a first-year to pick something they'd still enjoy if the job changed, and to learn how to explain things clearly. Explaining is a skill that holds its value, and I wish I'd practised it earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a first-year student starting your course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get an internship in year two, and don't rely on the course alone. And don't treat the tools as cheating, or as magic.

say: I'd say it's the one case where we can **get it right** with training and income rules.
I'd tell first-years to learn **explaining**, since it holds its value.
think: Ten years is enough for a **real career** first, perhaps senior by 34.
The AI would be one more tool, and my anxiety a **normal** kind.
do: Take a first job and learn **one new tool** every couple of months.
Get the debt **below 10,000** within five years.
feel: **Fine**, with a normal anxiety in the background.
S4.quote: Explaining is a skill that holds its value, and I wish I'd practised it earlier.
fieldNote: With a decade, Aisha sounds like a **normal** careful graduate, not a frightened one.
She plans a second field, psychology, as a hedge.
Debt target is clear: under 10,000 in five years.

steps.text: Take a first data job and keep it for at least two years
Learn one new AI tool every couple of months
Pay the debt below 10,000 within five years
Start a part-time psychology degree after the first year of work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no way I'd be ready. What would help is a hardship fund that doesn't need paperwork for weeks, retraining money that isn't tied to debt, and employers required to say when they're replacing roles with software. And more graduate schemes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against the technology. I use it, and I think it's good for many things. But I'd like someone in charge to be asking what happens to people like me, and I'm not sure anyone is.

headlineQuote: I'm not against the technology. I use it, and I think it's good for many things.
portrait: Aisha is 24, doing a **data science master's** after software engineering, with 28,000 of debt and three weeks of rent saved.
She tutors for 14 an hour; her freight firm internship was the **cleaning and reporting** that software takes first.
She is progressive, wants rules, and uses AI **now and then**, carefully, with her supervisor watching.
She is anxious in most worlds and **alarmed** at two years, when she'd drop the field and move to her aunt's.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she would not be ready and has no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a quick **hardship fund**, retraining money not tied to debt and employers who must disclose AI replacement.
